# Scalable Data Wrangling with Polars and Dask

##### The 40-node cluster that lost to a laptop

A team in Gurugram provisioned a Dask cluster to process 14 GB of clickstream data. Forty workers, ₹28,000 a month, and a two-week setup effort.

An engineer ran the same aggregation in Polars on his laptop. It finished in 22 seconds.

The 14 GB was a CSV. Converted to Parquet with sensible dtypes it was 2.1 GB, and Polars' streaming engine handled it comfortably in 16 GB of RAM using all eight cores.

Distribution has real overhead — serialisation, network transfer, scheduler coordination, worker startup. Below a threshold that is much higher than most people assume, a single machine with a good engine wins decisively.

Today is about knowing where that threshold sits, and about the two tools that push it much further than Pandas can.

##### Where Pandas actually breaks

Pandas has three structural limits, and only one of them is about size.

**Single-threaded.** Almost every Pandas operation uses one core. A groupby on an eight-core machine uses one-eighth of the available compute.

**Eager.** Every operation executes immediately, materialising a full intermediate result. A chain of five filters creates five DataFrames.

**Memory-hungry.** The rough guide is 5–10× the file size for CSV, because of object dtypes and intermediates during operations.

The escalation ladder, in the order you should actually try things:

| Situation | Action | Typical gain |
|---|---|---|
| Any size | Fix dtypes (`category`, `float32`, `usecols`) | 3–30× memory |
| Any size | Convert CSV to Parquet | 3–10× I/O |
| Under ~RAM/5 | Stay on Pandas | — |
| ~RAM/5 to 10× RAM | **Polars** (lazy, streaming) | 5–30× speed |
| 10× RAM, one machine | Polars streaming, or DuckDB | Bounded memory |
| Genuinely needs a cluster | **Dask** or Spark | Horizontal scale |

The Gurugram team skipped four rungs. **Escalate one step at a time and measure.**

##### Polars: eager vs lazy

Polars is a Rust DataFrame library on Apache Arrow. Two things make it fundamentally faster than Pandas: it is multithreaded by default, and its lazy API optimises a query plan before executing anything.

**Eager mode** behaves like Pandas — each operation runs immediately:

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.read_parquet("transactions.parquet")        # read_ = eager, loads now
result = (
    df.filter(pl.col("amount_inr") > 100)
      .group_by("city")
      .agg(pl.col("amount_inr").sum().alias("revenue"))
)
```

**Lazy mode** builds a plan and executes only on `collect()`:

```python
q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("transactions.parquet")          # scan_ = lazy, nothing loads
      .filter(pl.col("amount_inr") > 100)
      .filter(pl.col("city").is_in(["Pune", "Mumbai", "Bengaluru"]))
      .with_columns([
          pl.col("ts").dt.convert_time_zone("Asia/Kolkata").alias("ts_ist"),
          pl.col("amount_inr").log1p().alias("log_amount"),
      ])
      .group_by(["city", pl.col("ts_ist").dt.date()])
      .agg([
          pl.col("amount_inr").sum().alias("gmv"),
          pl.col("customer_id").n_unique().alias("dau"),
      ])
)

print(q.explain())                        # inspect the optimised plan
df = q.collect()                          # execute
df = q.collect(engine="streaming")        # execute with bounded memory
```

The optimiser applies three transformations you get for free:

**Predicate pushdown** — filters move into the Parquet reader, so rejected row groups are never decompressed. Reading a year's data and filtering to one month may touch only one twelfth of the file.

**Projection pushdown** — only columns the query actually uses are read off disk. On a forty-column table where you use six, that is a 7× I/O reduction with no code change.

**Common subexpression elimination** — an expression computed twice is computed once.

Reading `q.explain()` is worth doing at least once. You will see `SELECTION` and `PROJECTION` clauses appearing *inside* the scan node, which is the optimiser doing its work.

##### The Polars expression API

The expression system is where Polars diverges most from Pandas, and where it becomes genuinely more capable.

```python
result = (
    pl.scan_parquet("txns.parquet")
    .with_columns([
        # Window functions inside an expression — no separate groupby
        pl.col("amount_inr").mean().over("customer_id").alias("customer_avg"),
        pl.col("amount_inr").rank(descending=True).over("city").alias("rank_in_city"),
        (pl.col("amount_inr") / pl.col("amount_inr").sum().over("city") * 100)
            .alias("pct_of_city"),

        # Rolling windows, group-aware
        pl.col("amount_inr").rolling_mean(window_size=7).over("customer_id")
            .alias("amt_7d_avg"),

        # Conditional logic
        pl.when(pl.col("amount_inr") > 50_000).then(pl.lit("premium"))
          .when(pl.col("amount_inr") > 2_000).then(pl.lit("standard"))
          .otherwise(pl.lit("small")).alias("tier"),

        # String and date operations
        pl.col("city").str.to_lowercase().str.strip_chars().alias("city_clean"),
        pl.col("ts").dt.hour().alias("hour"),
    ])
    .filter(pl.col("rank_in_city") <= 100)
    .collect(engine="streaming")
)
```

`pl.col("amount").mean().over("customer_id")` is the operation that takes a groupby-transform-merge in Pandas and expresses it as one expression. Several such expressions in a single `with_columns` call are computed **in parallel** across threads.

Selectors make column-wise operations concise:

```python
import polars.selectors as cs

df.select(cs.numeric().mean())                    # mean of every numeric column
df.with_columns(cs.float().cast(pl.Float32))      # downcast all floats
df.select(cs.string() | cs.temporal())            # combine selectors
```

Two conversion notes. Polars-to-Pandas is nearly free thanks to Arrow: `df.to_pandas(use_pyarrow_extension_array=True)`. And the common production pattern is **Polars for the heavy ETL, then `.to_pandas()` on the small model-ready table**, because scikit-learn and the plotting ecosystem still assume Pandas.

##### Dask: parallel and out-of-core

Dask parallelises the Pandas API across cores or machines, and handles data larger than memory by processing it in partitions.

```python
import dask.dataframe as dd
from dask.distributed import Client

client = Client(n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=2, memory_limit="6GB")
print(client.dashboard_link)                       # genuinely useful for debugging

ddf = dd.read_parquet(
    "s3://data/txns/year=2026/",
    columns=["customer_id", "city", "ts", "amount_inr"],   # projection
    filters=[("amount_inr", ">", 0)],                      # predicate pushdown
)

print(ddf.npartitions)
print(ddf.dtypes)                                  # metadata only — no compute yet

daily = (ddf.assign(day=ddf.ts.dt.floor("D"))
            .groupby(["city", "day"])
            .amount_inr
            .sum())

result = daily.compute()                           # triggers the graph, returns Pandas
```

Dask splits data into partitions — each an in-memory Pandas DataFrame — builds a task graph, and executes it with a scheduler that spills to disk under pressure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Parquet files] --> B[Partition 1]
    A --> C[Partition 2]
    A --> D[Partition N]
    B --> E[map: filter + assign]
    C --> F[map: filter + assign]
    D --> G[map: filter + assign]
    E --> H{{shuffle by city, day}}
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I[reduce: sum]
    I --> J[compute - Pandas result]
```

The rules that determine whether Dask works well:

**Partition size of 100–500 MB.** Too small and scheduler overhead dominates; too large and workers run out of memory. Check with `ddf.map_partitions(len).compute()`.

**Call `.compute()` exactly once**, at the end. Calling it inside a loop re-executes the whole graph each time — the most common Dask performance bug.

**Use `persist()` for expensive intermediates** you will reuse:

```python
cleaned = ddf.dropna(subset=["customer_id"]).persist()   # keep in cluster memory
a = cleaned.groupby("city").amount_inr.sum().compute()
b = cleaned.groupby("day").amount_inr.mean().compute()
```

**Treat shuffles as expensive.** `set_index`, wide `groupby` and joins on unsorted keys move data across workers. Minimising them is most of Dask tuning.

For the simplest case — a larger-than-memory file you just need to aggregate — chunked Pandas is often enough and much simpler:

```python
totals = pd.Series(dtype=float)
for chunk in pd.read_csv("huge.csv", chunksize=500_000,
                         usecols=["city", "amount_inr"],
                         dtype={"city": "category"}):
    totals = totals.add(chunk.groupby("city", observed=True)["amount_inr"].sum(),
                        fill_value=0)
```

Reach for Dask when you need genuine parallelism or a cluster, not merely out-of-core.

##### DuckDB, briefly

Worth knowing as a third option that often beats both. DuckDB is an embedded columnar SQL engine that queries Parquet in place, uses all cores, and spills to disk:

```python
import duckdb

df = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT city, date_trunc('day', ts) AS day,
           SUM(amount_inr) AS gmv, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS dau
    FROM read_parquet('data/txns/**/*.parquet')
    WHERE amount_inr > 0
    GROUP BY 1, 2
""").df()
```

No server, no cluster, and if you already think in SQL it needs no new API. For aggregation over Parquet at 1 GB to a few hundred GB, it is frequently the fastest path.

##### Benchmarking honestly

```python
import time, psutil, os

def benchmark(fn, label, *args, **kwargs):
    proc = psutil.Process(os.getpid())
    mem_before = proc.memory_info().rss / 1e9
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args, **kwargs)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    mem_peak = proc.memory_info().rss / 1e9
    print(f"{label:22s} {elapsed:7.2f}s   peak RSS {mem_peak:5.2f} GB "
          f"(+{mem_peak - mem_before:.2f})")
    return out

pandas_result = benchmark(pandas_pipeline, "Pandas")
polars_result = benchmark(polars_pipeline, "Polars (lazy+stream)")
dask_result   = benchmark(dask_pipeline, "Dask (4 workers)")
```

Four rules for a benchmark anyone should believe. **Verify the outputs match** — a fast wrong answer is not a result, so sort and compare. **Include I/O**, because reading is often the dominant cost and it is where Polars and Dask gain most. **Measure memory**, not just time, since memory is usually the binding constraint. And **run at production scale** — a 100 MB benchmark measures startup overhead, and Pandas will win it.

Also account for developer time honestly. Polars requires learning a new API. Dask requires operating a cluster. A 3× speedup that costs two weeks of learning is not always the right trade.

##### Choosing

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S{Data size vs RAM} -->|Under 20% of RAM| P[Pandas - richest ecosystem]
    S -->|Comparable to RAM| PL[Polars lazy + streaming]
    S -->|10x RAM, one machine| PL2[Polars streaming or DuckDB]
    S -->|100x RAM or needs a cluster| D[Dask distributed]
    P --> N[Still slow? Fix dtypes and remove apply first]
    PL --> Q[Already SQL-shaped? Try DuckDB]
    PL2 --> Q
```

| | Pandas | Polars | Dask | DuckDB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parallelism | Single-threaded | Multi-core | Multi-core / cluster | Multi-core |
| Lazy optimisation | No | Yes | Partial | Yes |
| Larger than memory | No | Streaming | Yes | Yes (spills) |
| API | Familiar | New, expression-based | Pandas-like | SQL |
| Ecosystem | Enormous | Growing | Good | SQL tools |
| Ops complexity | None | None | **Real** | None |
| Sweet spot | < 5 GB | 1 GB – 100 GB | Cluster scale | Parquet + SQL |

The practical recommendation: **fix your dtypes and convert to Parquet first.** Then try Polars lazy. Only reach for Dask when you genuinely need a cluster — and measure before and after, so you can prove it.

##### Common mistakes

- Provisioning a cluster before checking `memory_usage(deep=True)`.
- Using `read_parquet` instead of `scan_parquet` in Polars, losing all pushdown.
- Mixing eager and lazy Polars and losing the optimisation.
- Calling `.compute()` inside a loop in Dask.
- Dask partitions of 5 MB or 8 GB.
- Not calling `persist()` on a reused intermediate.
- Forgetting `observed=True` on categorical groupbys after converting from Pandas.
- Benchmarking on 100 MB and extrapolating.
- Comparing runtimes without verifying the outputs match.
- Ignoring the operational cost of a distributed system in the comparison.

##### Hands-on

Rewrite a Pandas aggregation pipeline in Polars using `scan_parquet` and lazy execution, then print `explain()` and identify where predicate and projection pushdown appear in the plan. Separately, process a larger-than-memory CSV with chunked Pandas and with Dask, comparing runtime and peak memory. Verify all three produce identical results by sorting and using `assert_frame_equal`.

For the mini-project, build the same analytical pipeline three ways — Pandas, Polars lazy, and Dask — on a dataset large enough that the differences are real (a few gigabytes at minimum; generate synthetic data if needed). Produce a benchmark table covering runtime, peak memory, lines of code, and setup effort. Add a scaling plot: run each at 10%, 50% and 100% of the data and plot runtime against size, which reveals the crossover point where each tool starts to win. Finish with a written recommendation naming the size threshold at which you would switch, based on your own measurements rather than general advice.

For the assignment, explain the difference between Polars eager and lazy execution with a concrete example, and describe why lazy can be faster. Show the same query written both ways, include the `explain()` output, and point specifically at the pushdown that eager mode cannot perform.

##### Key takeaways

- Escalate one rung at a time: dtypes, then Parquet, then Polars, then a cluster — most teams skip four steps.
- Polars' lazy API optimises before executing; predicate and projection pushdown are free wins Pandas cannot offer.
- The Polars expression system computes multiple window and rolling operations in parallel within one call.
- Dask scales the Pandas API out-of-core and across machines; partition size and shuffle count decide whether it performs.
- Benchmark at production scale with memory *and* time, verify outputs match, and count operational cost in the comparison.
